pulses-mission-one-year.title: Pulses mission at one year: where the ₹11,440 crore is going
pulses-mission-one-year.deck: India grows more pulses than any other country and still imports them. The mission's first-year numbers show which part of that gap is closing and which is not.
pulses-mission-one-year.oneLine: The mission backs three pulses (tur, urad, masoor) with better seed, cluster farming and assured procurement at MSP, aiming for about 350 lakh tonnes of output by 2030-31.
pulses-mission-one-year.subject: Economy › Agriculture

whyInNews.text: PIB published a backgrounder on 11 October 2026 marking the first year of the Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses. The mission was launched on 11 October 2025 with ₹11,440 crore for 2025-26 to 2030-31.

sections.heading: Why does the world's largest producer still need imports?

body.text: Production is rising, but it started from a level that did not meet demand. Output reached 274.09 lakh tonnes in 2025-26 (3rd Advance Estimates), up from 256.83 lakh tonnes the year before. The mission's target is nearly 350 lakh tonnes by 2030-31.

body.label: Yield is the weak point.
body.text: National yield rose from 926 to 957 kg per hectare in 2025-26. The mission wants 1,130 kg per hectare, so most of the extra output has to come from each hectare rather than from new land.

body.label: Area is growing too.
body.text: Pulse area went from 277.20 to 286.46 lakh hectares. The target is 310 lakh hectares by 2030-31.

body.label: The import bill is shrinking.
body.text: Imports fell from ₹46,427.60 crore in 2024-25 to ₹31,793.59 crore in 2025-26, a decline of 31.52%.

sections.heading: How does the mission try to raise output?

body.label: Three crops, not all pulses.
body.text: The focus is tur, urad and masoor, the pulses India most often falls short on.

body.label: Seed first.
body.text: It plans 87.5 lakh free seed kits and 126 lakh quintals of certified seed over six years. During Rabi 2025-26, 9.25 lakh kits went out, aimed at rice-fallow land that would otherwise sit idle after the paddy harvest.

body.label: Clusters.
body.text: Production is concentrated in 489 districts so that extension, seed and procurement reach the same farms.

body.label: Processing.
body.text: The mission envisages 1,000 dal mills; 528 have been allocated to States and UTs in the first phase.

body.label: Tracking.
body.text: The SATHI portal traces seed from production to sale, and the Krishi Mapper app geo-tags demonstration plots.

sections.heading: Why does assured procurement matter more than a higher MSP?

body.text: An MSP only protects a farmer if someone actually buys at that price. Wheat and rice have that buyer; pulses mostly have not, which is one reason farmers have preferred cereals.

Under the mission, NCCF and NAFED may buy 100% of tur, masur and urad offered by registered farmers for four years (2025-26 to 2028-29). Pulses procurement rose from 18,39,504.77 tonnes in 2024-25 to 31,40,883.92 tonnes in 2025-26.

body.label: MSP did rise as well.
body.text: Urad went from ₹7,400 to ₹8,200 per quintal (10.81%), tur from ₹7,550 to ₹8,450 (11.92%) and masur from ₹6,700 to ₹7,000 (4.48%) between 2024-25 and 2026-27.

pulses-mission-one-year.misconception: The 31.52% fall is in the value of imports in rupees. The release does not give import tonnage, so do not write that import volumes fell by a third.

back2basics.text: MSP is a price the Union government announces before sowing, on the recommendation of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP). It is a floor only where a public agency is ready to buy. NAFED and NCCF are cooperative federations the government uses as procurement agencies for pulses and oilseeds.

mcq.stem:
With reference to the Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses, consider the following statements:
1. NCCF and NAFED are authorised to procure 100% of tur, urad and masoor from registered farmers for four years.
2. The mission's outlay covers 2025-26 to 2030-31.
3. The mission targets a national pulse yield of 1,130 kg per hectare by 2030-31.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcq.trap: Statement 1 invites rejection because procurement is usually capped. For these three pulses it is 100%, but only for 2025-26 to 2028-29, not the whole mission period. A question could swap those years.

mains.label: Practice question
mains.question: Assured procurement may do more for self-sufficiency in pulses than a higher MSP alone. Examine with reference to the Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses.
mains.demand: Explain why a support price works only when there is a buyer, use the mission's data, and judge whether procurement is enough without higher yields.

structure.intro: India is the largest producer of pulses yet imports them; the mission targets about 350 lakh tonnes by 2030-31.
body: Why MSP alone has not shifted farmers away from wheat and rice
The 100% procurement mandate for tur, urad and masoor and the rise in procurement
Supporting levers: seed kits, cluster districts, dal mills
Limit: yield of 957 kg/ha against a 1,130 kg/ha target
structure.conclusion: Procurement buys farmer confidence; yield decides whether self-sufficiency lasts.

pyq.question: What do you mean by Minimum Support Price (MSP)? How will MSP rescue the farmers from the low-income trap?
pyq.why: Same mechanism. The 2018 question asks how MSP lifts farm incomes; the pulses mission is a live test of MSP backed by assured procurement.

faq.a: On 11 October 2025, with ₹11,440 crore for 2025-26 to 2030-31.

faq.q: Which pulses does it focus on?
What does '3rd Advance Estimates' mean for the 274.09 lakh tonne figure?
faq.a: It is the third provisional estimate for 2025-26, not the final number, so it can still be revised.

sources.title: India's Mission for Aatmanirbharta in Pulses (PIB Backgrounder)

nba-abs-disbursal.title: Rs 2.02 crore from seed companies: how biodiversity benefit-sharing works
nba-abs-disbursal.deck: Companies that use India's biological resources pay a share back. This round shows who receives it when the original growers cannot be traced.
nba-abs-disbursal.oneLine: Under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, firms that use biological resources pay Access and Benefit-Sharing (ABS) contributions, which the NBA passes to state boards for conservation and local communities.
nba-abs-disbursal.subject: Environment › Biodiversity

whyInNews.text: On 10 October 2026 the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) disbursed Rs 2.02 crore of ABS contributions from seed-sector companies to 27 State Biodiversity Boards and 3 Union Territory Biodiversity Councils. Its cumulative ABS disbursement has now reached Rs 202.00 crore.

sections.heading: Where does the money come from?

body.text: From seed companies that used Indian agricultural biological resources to develop varieties and hybrids of rice, eggplant, cauliflower, cucumber, hot pepper, bottle gourd, bitter gourd, tomato and okra.

body.label: The payers.
body.text: East West Seeds India, Syngenta India, Devgen Seeds and Crop Technology, Limagrain India, Bayer Science & Innovation, Nunhems India and Enza Zaden India.

body.label: The principle.
body.text: A company that profits from a biological resource shares part of that benefit with the people and places that conserved it. That is the 'benefit-sharing' half of ABS; the 'access' half is the approval needed before using the resource.

sections.heading: Who receives it when the growers cannot be identified?

body.text: Much of this material was bought through markets or traders, so no individual farmer or community could be named as the source. For such cases the NBA used distribution rules recommended by an expert committee.

body.label: The formula.
body.text: The beneficiary share was split among state boards in proportion to the area under each crop, using the Ministry of Agriculture's statistics.

body.label: The result.
body.text: Madhya Pradesh received the largest share, Rs 23,81,072, and the top 10 States together received Rs 1.43 crore.

body.label: What this means.
body.text: Cultivation area is a stand-in for 'who conserved this crop'. It sends money to the right states, but not necessarily to the specific communities that kept a variety alive.

sections.heading: What is the money meant to pay for?

body.text: State boards use it to strengthen Biodiversity Management Committees, update People's Biodiversity Registers, conserve traditional crop varieties and medicinal plants, and restore habitats.

body.label: Convergence.
body.text: The NBA suggests linking these activities with PM-JANMAN, the Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Vikas Mission and the Pradhan Mantri Van Dhan Yojana.

sections.heading: How does this connect to India's global commitments?

body.text: The release ties the ABS framework to the National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan 2024–2030 and to two targets of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework: Target 13 on fair sharing of benefits from genetic resources and traditional knowledge, and Target 19 on resource mobilisation.
It comes just before COP 17 of the Convention on Biological Diversity, which begins on 19 October 2026 in Yerevan, Armenia.

nba-abs-disbursal.misconception: ABS is not a royalty paid to individual farmers by default. Where no individual claimant can be identified, the share goes to state boards and councils, not to a central fund.

keyNumbers.meaning: State Biodiversity Boards and UT Biodiversity Councils that received shares
Cumulative ABS disbursed by the NBA

back2basics.text: The Act sets up three tiers: the National Biodiversity Authority (headquartered in Chennai), State Biodiversity Boards, and Biodiversity Management Committees at the level of local bodies, which keep People's Biodiversity Registers. It is how India implements the Convention on Biological Diversity and its Nagoya Protocol on access and benefit-sharing.

mcq.stem:
Consider the following statements about Access and Benefit-Sharing (ABS) in India:
1. ABS contributions are disbursed by the National Biodiversity Authority to State Biodiversity Boards.
2. Target 13 of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework concerns fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources.
3. Where individual benefit claimers cannot be identified, the benefit share lapses to the Consolidated Fund of India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcq.trap: Statement 3 sounds administratively neat. In this disbursal the NBA instead shared the money among state boards by cultivation area.

mains.label: Practice question
mains.question: Access and benefit-sharing is meant to reward the communities that conserve biological resources. Examine how far India's ABS mechanism achieves this, with reference to a recent disbursement.
mains.demand: Explain the mechanism, test the 'reward communities' claim against how the money was actually distributed, and conclude.

structure.intro: Define ABS under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 and the Nagoya Protocol.
body: Who pays: seed companies using crops such as rice, tomato and okra
Who receives when claimants are unknown: an area-based formula for state boards
End use: Biodiversity Management Committees, People's Biodiversity Registers, traditional varieties
Limit: the area formula reaches states, not necessarily the conserving communities
structure.conclusion: Better People's Biodiversity Registers would let more benefits reach identified communities; link to Target 13 and COP 17.

faq.q: Which companies paid in this round?
faq.a: East West Seeds India, Syngenta India, Devgen Seeds and Crop Technology, Limagrain India, Bayer Science & Innovation, Nunhems India and Enza Zaden India.

sources.title: NBA disburses Rs 2.02 crore of ABS funds from seed sector

ibca-new-office.title: International Big Cat Alliance: India's treaty body for seven big cats
ibca-new-office.deck: The alliance opened a new office in Delhi this week. For the exam, what matters is what kind of body it is, who has joined, and how it fits alongside India's other alliances.
ibca-new-office.oneLine: IBCA is a treaty-based inter-governmental organisation headquartered in India for conserving seven big cats; 29 countries are members and India has pledged Rs 150 crore for five years.
ibca-new-office.subject: Environment › Conservation; IR › Groupings

whyInNews.text: On 12 October 2026 the Union Environment Minister inaugurated new office premises for the International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA) at 55 Lodhi Estate, New Delhi. Heads of the International Solar Alliance, the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure and the Global Biofuels Alliance attended.

sections.heading: What kind of body is IBCA?

body.text: It is a treaty-based inter-governmental organisation with its headquarters in India. Its mandate covers seven big cats: lion, tiger, leopard, snow leopard, cheetah, jaguar and puma.

body.label: Why the list matters.
body.text: Jaguar and puma are found only in the Americas, so the alliance needs range countries far beyond Asia and Africa to mean anything for those species.

sections.heading: Who has joined, and who pays?

body.label: Members.
body.text: 29 countries, including India, are members. Another 5 are observers and 11 more have consented to join.

body.label: Money.
body.text: India has pledged an initial Rs 150 crore for five years, 2023-24 to 2027-28.

sections.heading: What has it done in its first two and a half years?

body.label: Training.
body.text: Two capacity-building programmes under the MEA's ITEC scheme, and a PRIME cat health programme for veterinary doctors from 20 countries.

body.label: Diplomacy.
body.text: Participation in the CITES COP, the CITES Standing Committee and the UNFCCC COP.

body.label: What the release does not show.
body.text: Its list is of training and outreach. It reports no conservation outcomes, such as changes in big cat populations, so avoid claiming any.

sections.heading: How does it fit India's alliance diplomacy?

body.text: The guest list is the useful clue. The ISA, CDRI and the Global Biofuels Alliance are all issue-based bodies that India started or hosts. IBCA follows the same pattern: India hosts the secretariat, funds the early years and builds membership around a single global problem.

ibca-new-office.misconception: IBCA is not part of CITES or the IUCN. It is a separate treaty-based organisation headquartered in India, which takes part in CITES and UNFCCC meetings.

keyNumbers.meaning: Observers / countries that have consented to join
Countries whose vets joined the PRIME cat health programme

back2basics.text: Project Tiger and Project Cheetah are India's domestic programmes; IBCA is the international layer built on that experience. The tiger is protected under Schedule I of the Wild Life (Protection) Act and listed in CITES Appendix I, which bans commercial international trade.

mcq.stem:
Consider the following statements about the International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA):
1. It is a treaty-based inter-governmental organisation headquartered in India.
2. Its mandate covers seven big cat species, including the jaguar and the puma.
3. Membership is restricted to countries where big cats occur naturally.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcq.trap: Statement 3 adds a restriction that sounds logical. IBCA is open to non-range countries too, and UPSC often tests invented restrictions like this.

mains.label: Practice question
mains.question: India has founded or hosts several issue-based international alliances, such as the ISA, CDRI, the Global Biofuels Alliance and the International Big Cat Alliance. Discuss what this approach offers India's foreign policy and where it falls short.
mains.demand: Explain why India uses single-issue coalitions, give evidence from IBCA, and assess limits honestly.

structure.intro: Issue-based coalitions as a tool alongside formal groupings like the UN and G20.
body: Agenda-setting: secretariats hosted in India (IBCA headquarters)
South-South capacity building: ITEC programmes, vets from 20 countries
Commitment signal: India's Rs 150 crore pledge
Limit: outputs so far are training and outreach; outcomes are yet to be shown
structure.conclusion: Judge these alliances by results and adoption, not by membership counts.

faq.q: Which seven big cats does IBCA cover?
faq.a: Lion, tiger, leopard, snow leopard, cheetah, jaguar and puma.
29 members including India, with 5 observers and 11 more that have consented to join.

sources.title: Union Environment Minister inaugurates new office premises of International Big Cat Alliance
